newsitem.title: HAITI: Disney charged with using Haiti sweatshops.
newsitem.headline: Disney charged with using Haiti sweatshops.

text.p: A U.S.-based Haitian rights organisation on Wednesday accused Walt Disney Co and other U.S. firms of using Haitian sweatshops to make products sold in the United States.

"The minimum wage, which in any case is not enough to live on,is sometimes not paid. Daily piecework quotas are unrealistic and frequently raised if they are met. Workers who don't make the quota are first reprimanded and then fired. Sexual harassment is frequent. Workers who attempt to organise are fired," said a statement by the Washington Office on Haiti.

"Haiti's Labour Code is seldom adhered to and the Labour Court ineffective," the group said, after interviews with workers and an investigation of manufacturing facilities in Haiti producing garments sold by Disney, Wal-Mart Stores Inc, Kmart Corp and other U.S. firms.
On Tuesday, shareholders at Disney's annual meeting presented a proposal, which was overwhelmingly defeated, calling for setting up higher standards at contract suppliers.

Earlier this month, unions in Britain, joined by the actress Julie Christie, called for a boycott of Disney stores over the alleged exploitation of workers in Haiti. And in December, the New York-based National Labour Committee organised protests at Disney stores over alleged worker abuse.

Disney has denied that its plants in Haiti, the hemisphere's poorest nation with an estimated 80 percent unemployment rate and a minimum wage of $0.28 per hour, were marked by poor conditions. Wal-Mart had no immediate comment and Kmart did not immediately return calls for comment.
"There are no sweatshops being used by any of our licensees or by our direct sourcing organisation anywhere," said Disney spokesman John Dreyer from the company's offices in California.

After a week of interviews and visits to plants, the Washington Office on Haiti said conditions in Haitian sweatshops stiching up garments for sale at Disney stores, Wal-Mart Stores Inc and K-Mart Corp are "extremely exploitative."

The Washington Office on Haiti called the labour conditions part of a U.S.-led economic programme for Haiti that is "pushing Haiti down a path that can never lead to real development for the Haitian people. If followed, its direction will bring Haiti to economic, environmental and social disaster."
Officials at the U.S. embassy in Port-au-Prince said they could offer no immediate comment.

The Disney spokesman said the company had inspected the plants in Haiti three times, the U.S. embassy had inspected them and a commission of Haitian unions, manufacturers and the government had inspected them. Workers at the Disney plants in Haiti are paid $0.48- $0.52 per hour.

At Disney's annual meeting, one demonstrator held a sign comparing wages in Haiti with the pay of Disney Chief Executive Michael Eisner. The sign read, "It would take a Haitian 16.8 years to earn Eisner's hourly income of $9,783.00."
Walt Disney Co. shareholders on Tuesday approved a new 10-year contract for Eisner that critics claim could be worth as much as $400 million.
